DI G Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph DILG OPINION NO. 35 s. 2021 Mar. 5, 2021 HON. ANTONIO R. CEBALLOS Vice Mayor Pilar, Cebu Dear Vice-Mayor Ceballos: This has reference to your request for clarification regarding the following matters: 1. Hiring of private lawyers to defray litigation expenses on legal actions where the adverse party is/are elected govemment officials or that between local government units; 2. Sufficiency of resolution to realign funds from the MOOE for the above purpose; 3. Non-observance of requirements set in COA Circular No. 98-002; 4. LCE prerogative to prevent Department Heads to appear before the Sangguniang Bayan session to clarify matters of public interest; 5. Centralizing the hiring of Jos including those under the Office of the Vice Mayor a. Relief from approval of majority of the members of the Sangguniang Bayan; and b. Relief from LCE's action. As a background, a request seeking guidance has been submitted before DILG Regional Office, Region VII relative to the abovementioned concerns, to which the Regional Office accordingly acted upon, in a letter dated 06 October 2020. Nonetheless, Regional Director Leocadio T. Trovela, DILG Region VII, seeks the guidance from the Central Office. It is observed that the first, second and third issues are interrelated. Hence, we shall discuss the same jointly. This Department subscribes to the position given by the Regional Office anent the possibility of hiring private lawyers. Nevertheless, kindly consider the foregoing as an additional basis for the position provided.

This Department, in DILG Legal Opinion No. 7, Series of 2011, had opined that: "As a general rule, a municipality cannot engage the services of a private lawyer. Only the Provincial Prosecutor, the Provincial Attomey or the Municipal Attomey could validly represent a municipality in all cases/complaints and legal problems involving it. The reason being that only accountable public officers may act for and in behalf of public entities and that public funds should not be expended to hire private lawyers (Ramos vs. Court of Appeals, 269 SCRA 34). Thus, in case of Ramos vs. COLM of Appeals, 108 SCRA 728, the Supreme COUN was rather emphatic when it declared that a private lawyer cannot represent a local government unit even if the services rendered was gratis, and stated that 'the municipality should not be burdened with expenses of hiring a private lawyer and that interests of the municipality would be best protected if a govemment lawyer handles its litigation. ' However, in the case of Mancenido, et.al vs. Court of Appeals, the Supreme Court enumerated several exceptions to the genera! rule discussed above, to wit: 1. Only when the provincial fiscal is disqualified may the municipal council be authorized to hire the services of a special attorney; 2. The provincial public prosecutor is disqualified from representing a particular municipality: (a) when the jurisdiction of a case involving the municipalities lies with the Supreme Court; (b) when the municipality is a party adverse to the Provincial Government or to some other municipality in the same province; and (c) when in a case involving the municipality, the provincial prosecutor, his spouse, or his child is involved as a creditor, heir, legatee or otherwise; 3. In resolving whether a local government official may secure the sen.'ices of a private counsel in an action filed against him in his official capacity, the nature of the action and the relief sought are to be considered. " We do not see any reason to deviate from the previous position rendered by this Department. However, when services of a private lawyer is unavoidable or is not justified under the exceptional circumstances, COA Circular No. 98-002 is instructive, which states that "with respect to local government units, only in those instances provided in paragraph 3(1) of Section 481 of RA 7160, which states, thus: 'xxx Provided, that, in actions or proceedings where a component city or municipality is a party

adverse to the provincial government or to another component city or municipality, a special legal officer may be employed to represent the adverse party, ' may public funds be utilized for the services of a private legal counsel or law firm". In connection thereto, a Memorandum issued by the Commission on Audit (COA), entitled "Revised Guidelines on Deputation of Private Lawyers and Special Attorneys" provides the guidelines on deputation of private lawyers and special attorneys. Moreover, in hiring private lawyers, the same requires the prior written conformity and acquiescence of the Office of the Solicitor General and the written concurrence of COA before the hiring of private lawyers and law firms. Thus, assuming there is an exceptional need to hire a private lawyer, it must be noted that the appropriation ordinance is controlling to determine if there is a provision therein which specifically covers the expenses to be incurred in hiring a private lawyer. On the contrary, a specific sanggunian approval, which should be in the form of an ordinance, may be required for the payment due to the aforesaid lawyer if the latter's services are neither specified in the appropriation ordinance nor encompassed within the regular personal services and maintenance and other operating expenses. As regards the fourth query, we defer to the position given by the Regional Office on the matter. Lastly, with respect to the fifth query, we likewise adopt the opinion of the Regional Office. And in addition, DILG Opinion No. 17, Series of 2010 finds application, wherein this Department posits that: "With respect to the casual and job order employees, we have to qualify. As also contained in our Opinion No. 32, series of 2005 dated June 8, 2005, we considered job order employees as among those falling under the second type of casual employees. Thus, we clarified therein that there are two (2) types of casual employees to wit: (a) those provided for in the plantilla of the local government unit concemed and filled up via "appointment", and (b) those not provided for in the plantilla and hired through job order contracts. In the first type of casual employees, we were, and we still are, ofthe view that the Vice Mayor has the authority to appoint them. In the second type, on the other hand, the Mayor has the authority to hire them through the execution of job order contracts. This is because while there is nothing in the LGC that confers authority upon the Vice Mayor to sign any contract,

Section 77 of the LGC explicitly confers authority upon the local chief executive to hire workers through job order contracts. Thus, with respect to casual positions not provided for in the plantilla and are to be hired through job order contracts, the authority to hire them is lodged with the Mayor regardless of the source of their salaries. To opine differently would run counter to the explicit provision of the LGC as aforementioned which confers authority upon the local chief executive to hire job order employees. " This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have enlightened you on the matter. Very truly yours, uthority of the Secretary: 'NGAN, CESO Ill -in-Charge Office of the Undersecretary for Local Government Legal/91 Copy fumished: DIR. LEOCADIO T. TROVELA, CESO IV Regional Director, DILG-Region VII Sudlon, Lahug Cebu City
